title: Hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide
subtitle: SN1: ionise first, then add water

reactants.caption: tert-butyl bromide + water
reactants.learnerPrompt: The first step of SN1. Draw it.
hintTiers: A tertiary carbon is too crowded for backside attack. What can the C–Br bond do on its own?
The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically: both electrons go to bromine. One arrow.
The C–Br bond breaks, and its pair goes onto bromine, leaving a tertiary carbocation.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Three methyl groups block the back of this carbon, so water cannot attack it directly. The C–Br bond breaks first.
The C–Br pair goes to bromine, the more electronegative atom, leaving the carbon positive.

carbocation.caption: tert-butyl cation + bromide
carbocation.learnerPrompt: Water traps the carbocation. Draw the arrow.
hintTiers: The cation is flat, with an empty p orbital. Which species has a lone pair to fill it?
A lone pair on the oxygen of water forms a bond to the positive carbon. One arrow.
The lone pair on water's oxygen forms a new bond to the positive carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That simply re-forms tert-butyl bromide. It does happen, but water is present in huge excess and traps the cation as the alcohol.

oxonium-ion.caption: protonated tert-butanol + bromide
oxonium-ion.learnerPrompt: Turn the protonated alcohol into the neutral alcohol.
hintTiers: The O–H bond of a positively charged oxygen is acidic. Which molecule present can act as a base?
A second water takes the proton from the positive oxygen; the O–H pair stays on that oxygen. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: a lone pair of a second water forms a bond to the hydrogen on the positive oxygen. Arrow 2: that O–H bond breaks, and its pair goes back onto the oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Bromide is a very weak base (HBr is a strong acid). Water, the solvent, takes the proton.
Losing water just goes back to the cation. Removing a proton gives the neutral alcohol.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right base, right proton. Hydrogen can only have one bond: where does the old O–H pair go?

steps.explanationAfterStep: The slow, rate-determining step: the rate depends only on tert-butyl bromide. The tertiary cation is stabilised by hyperconjugation from the C–H bonds of its three methyl groups.
Water can attack either face of the flat cation, so a stereocentre here would be racemised. The oxygen now has three bonds and carries the positive charge.
A proton transfer gives tert-butanol and H₃O⁺. Overall, OH has replaced Br and HBr has formed.

mechanismSummary: SN1: slow ionisation to a tertiary carbocation (rate = k[t-BuBr]), then fast capture by water and loss of a proton. The intermediate is flat, so a stereocentre here would be racemised. Tertiary halides react this way because the cation is stable and the back of the carbon is blocked.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 15
